title: He Has Risen: Emmaus, the Upper Room, and the Ascension
summary: On the first day of the week the women find Jesus' tomb empty and hear from two angels that he has risen. That afternoon the risen Jesus walks unrecognized with two disciples to Emmaus, explains the Scriptures about himself, and is recognized in the breaking of bread. He then appears to the gathered disciples, shows them his hands and feet, eats before them, opens their minds to the Scriptures, commissions them as witnesses to all nations, and is carried up into heaven from near Bethany.
story: Everything in Luke has been moving toward Jerusalem, and here the story reaches its goal. The Jesus who was crucified and buried in chapter 23 is alive, and the chapter moves in a single day from confusion and grief to worship and great joy. The key to the whole chapter is Scripture: Jesus shows that his suffering and rising were written in Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms, and that the next chapter of the story is the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. Luke ends where he began, in the temple, with people praising God. His second volume, Acts, picks up exactly here, retelling the ascension (and making clear that the appearances continued over forty days, Acts 1:3) and following the witnesses from Jerusalem to Rome.
historical:
The Christian church confesses that Jesus of Nazareth rose bodily from the dead on the third day. That is first-order confession, not an optional extra, and Luke presents it as an event in history, set in a real place and on a particular morning. The historical evidence can be stated plainly. The earliest written witness is Paul's summary in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, written in the mid-50s AD, which passes on a tradition he had received, most scholars think within a few years of the crucifixion: that Christ died, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Peter, to the Twelve, to more than five hundred at once, to James, and to Paul himself. All four Gospels report that women discovered the empty tomb, a surprising detail for anyone inventing a story, since in that culture women's testimony carried less weight in public and legal matters. Jesus' disciples, who had fled and hidden, became bold public witnesses in the same city where he had been executed, and many suffered for it. Jewish believers began to gather for worship on the first day of the week.

Historians who do not share the church's faith generally accept that Jesus was crucified, that his followers soon afterward sincerely believed they had seen him alive, and that this conviction launched the Christian movement. Alternative explanations have been offered, including hallucinations, a stolen body, or the wrong tomb; each has been examined and answered at length. Luke does not argue the case by probabilities. He tells it as testimony, what the witnesses saw, heard, touched, and ate with.
cultural:
Jewish burial customs called for anointing the body with spices and perfumes, which the women had prepared but could not bring on the Sabbath. Emmaus was a village about seven miles (literally sixty stadia) from Jerusalem, and its exact location is uncertain; several sites have been proposed. Hospitality meant inviting a traveler to stay as evening fell. At the meal, the stranger takes the host's role, blessing and breaking the bread, and in that familiar act they know him.

The disciples' first fear, that they were seeing a spirit, reflects a widespread ancient belief in ghosts, the shades of the dead. Jesus answers it directly: a spirit does not have flesh and bones. Many Jews expected a resurrection of all the righteous at the end of the age, not the resurrection of one person in the middle of history, which is part of why the disciples were so slow to grasp what had happened. The phrase the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms names the three parts of the Hebrew Scriptures, the Psalms standing for the Writings.
literary: The chapter is a sequence of three scenes on one day: the empty tomb at dawn (verses 1 to 12), the road to Emmaus in the afternoon (verses 13 to 35), and the appearance to the gathered disciples in the evening, followed by the ascension (verses 36 to 53). Each scene moves from perplexity to understanding, and each turns on remembering or opening. The women remember his words; the Emmaus disciples' eyes are opened; the disciples' minds are opened to the Scriptures. The Emmaus story is a masterpiece of irony, with the risen Jesus hearing his own story told as a tragedy by people who do not recognize him. The chapter echoes the beginning of the Gospel, which also opened in the temple with worship. A few manuscripts, chiefly the Western text represented by Codex Bezae, lack verse 12, verse 40, and the words about Jesus being carried up into heaven in verse 51 and being worshiped in verse 52, but most scholars now accept these as original.

outline.t: Known in the breaking of the bread
Jesus appears to the disciples in the flesh
The Scriptures opened and the witnesses commissioned

doctrines.note: Jesus' resurrection is bodily: he has flesh and bones, bears the wounds of the cross, and eats fish. It is the firstfruits of the resurrection promised to his people and the ground of Christian hope that death will not have the last word over the body or the world.

The risen Jesus teaches that all of Scripture, Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms, speaks of him. He does not replace the Old Testament but interprets it, and the church has read it in his light ever since.

Repentance and forgiveness of sins are to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. The disciples are witnesses, and they are to wait for the promise of the Father, power from on high, which Acts will describe as the gift of the Holy Spirit.

words.note: Egeirō, to raise or rise. The angels say “He is not here; He has risen!” The verb here is passive in form and can be rendered he has been raised, pointing to God as the one who raised him. The New Testament speaks both of Jesus rising and of God raising him.

Diermēneuō, to interpret or explain thoroughly. Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, Jesus explained what was written in all the Scriptures about himself. It is built on the same root as the English word hermeneutics, the discipline of interpretation, and it makes the risen Jesus the church's first teacher of how to read the Old Testament.

Martus, witness. “You are witnesses of these things.” A witness testifies to what he has seen and heard, which is why the resurrection appearances matter. Because so many early witnesses died for their testimony, the word later came to mean martyr.

christ: This chapter shows Jesus as the living Lord, the same Jesus who was crucified, now raised in a real and transformed body. His wounds are still there; he eats, speaks, and blesses, yet he appears and disappears and is not always recognized at first. He interprets Israel's Scriptures as a single story that runs through the Christ's suffering to his glory. He sends his disciples to all nations and promises the Spirit. He blesses them with lifted hands, like a priest, and is carried into heaven, and they worship him, the right response to one who is Lord. The resurrection declares that Jesus' death was not defeat, that his claims were true, and that the new creation has begun.

hard.q: Did the resurrection really happen, or can it be explained another way?
hard.a: The question deserves a direct answer. The church confesses that Jesus rose bodily from the dead; this is the foundation of Christian faith, and Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:17). Several alternative explanations have been proposed. The disciples stole the body: but they then suffered for a claim they knew to be false. The women went to the wrong tomb: but the authorities could have produced the body. The appearances were hallucinations or visions: but hallucinations are private experiences, while the reports include groups, meals, and touching, and visions of a dead man would not by themselves have led first-century Jews to proclaim resurrection. The story grew as legend over time: but Paul's list of witnesses dates to within a few decades and rests on earlier tradition. Scholars such as N. T. Wright have argued at length that the empty tomb and the appearances together best explain the rise of the church's belief. Those who reject the resurrection often do so because they judge that the dead do not rise, a conviction that the evidence cannot settle by itself. Luke's account leaves the reader where it left the Emmaus disciples: with the Scriptures, the testimony of witnesses, and an invitation to recognize the risen one.

questions: The Emmaus disciples said, “But we were hoping.” Where have your hopes in God seemed to end in disappointment, and how might this story speak to that?
Jesus showed his wounds after he rose. What does it mean that the risen Christ still bears the marks of the cross?
The disciples' hearts burned as Jesus opened the Scriptures. What would help you read the Old Testament as a book that speaks of him?
